note: One sight-reading drill for wide leaps, a section per size: a tune with two 7ths, one with an octave up and down, one that leaps past the octave. Each is read from the staff before it is heard, then checked with Play; the why says how to find each leap from a note already known, each section has a fix for a leap that misses, and the key is moves, with a {{?key}} line on what stays the same.

exercise.title: Read tunes with wide leaps: a 7th, an octave and past it
exercise.why: A wide leap lands near a note you already hear: an octave is the same note higher or lower, a 7th is one step short of it and a 9th or 10th is the Re or Mi you know an octave up, so think the near note and the leap has a place to land.

cells.text:
Tap the first note of the tune below to hear it, before you press Play. The tune opens with Do up to Ti, a major 7th, and its second bar opens with Re up to the high Do, a minor 7th. Sing it from the staff on the note names, at your own pace.
Then press Play below to hear the tune: the mic starts with it. Check what you sang against it.
If Do up to Ti misses, sing Do up to the high Do and step down to Ti. Then sing the leap again and only think the high Do.

Tap the first note of the tune below to hear it. The tune opens with Do up to the high Do, and in its second bar Sol drops an octave to the Sol under Do. Sing it from the staff on the note names.
Then press Play below to hear the tune, and check where your line lands after each leap.
Practice until both leaps land without a slide.

Tap the first note of the tune below to hear it. The tune leaps from Do up to the high Re, a 9th, then settles on the high Do. Sing it from the staff on the note names.
Then press Play below to hear the tune, and check where your leap landed.
If the 9th misses, sing Do, Re and the high Re as three notes. Then leave out the middle one.
_If the top note strains, sing it softer, never louder._
{{?key}}In another key the notes are new, and each leap is still the same size.
